title: Two gold-plated records of Earth’s music are leaving the Solar System on the Voyagers

cover.alt: The golden Voyager record: a shining gold-plated disc with the words ‘The Sounds of Earth’ around its label, photographed against a dark background.

body: Each Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, carries a 12-inch copper phonograph record plated with nickel and then gold, its contents chosen by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan. The grooves hold an eclectic 90-minute selection of music, from Bach and a Navajo night chant to Chuck Berry’s ‘Johnny B. Goode’ and a Peruvian wedding song, plus spoken greetings in 55 languages, sounds such as surf, thunder and whale song, and 116 pictures encoded as sound. The aluminium cover explains in symbols how to play it at 16⅔ revolutions per minute, and carries a sample of uranium-238 so that a finder could work out its age. Voyager 1 will pass within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445 in roughly 40,000 years.

slides.alt: The engraved aluminium cover of the Voyager Golden Record, showing diagrams of the record and stylus, binary timing codes, a pulsar map and a hydrogen atom.
slides.caption: The record’s cover: instructions in symbols for playing it and decoding the pictures, and a pulsar map that locates the Sun.

slides.heading: Which track is longest?
slides.explanation: The Beethoven excerpt runs 8 min 50 s, the Bach 4:40, Chuck Berry 2:03 and the Navajo chant 57 s. In all, 27 pieces fill about 90 minutes.

slides.heading: What is on the record
items: 27 pieces of music from many cultures
An hour of Ann Druyan’s brainwaves, compressed to a minute

slides.question: How fast is the record meant to spin?
slides.explanation: Half the speed of an LP, which stretches the playing time: each side runs about 53 to 54 minutes. The cover gives the rotation time in units of a hydrogen transition.

left.label: The story
left.text: ‘Here Comes the Sun’ was considered, and Carl Sagan wrote that the Beatles liked the idea, but EMI, which held the copyright, declined.

right.label: The caveat
right.text: Ann Druyan said in 2015 that EMI wanted $50,000 per record; Timothy Ferris countered in 2017 that the song was never seriously considered.

slides.label: until Voyager 1 passes within about 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445
slides.text: By then the uranium-238 on the cover, with a half-life of 4.47 billion years, will have barely begun to decay.
